explain.say: Sound speed in the sea changes with depth. Near the surface warm water makes it fast; deeper, colder water slows it; and very deep down, huge pressure speeds it up again.

explain.say: That leaves a layer, often about a kilometre down, where sound is slowest. Sound waves bend towards slower water, so sound in this layer keeps curving back in and gets trapped: the SOFAR channel.

explain.say: Trapped sound spreads sideways instead of being lost at the surface or sea floor. The deep, low calls of fin and blue whales can be detected hundreds of kilometres away.

faq.a: The SOFAR channel, short for sound fixing and ranging, is a layer of ocean, often about a kilometre deep, where sound travels slowest. Sound bends back into it from above and below, so it is trapped and travels very far.
asks: What is the deep sound channel?
Why does sound get trapped in the ocean?

faq.q: How far can whale songs travel?
faq.a: The low calls of fin and blue whales can be detected by underwater microphones hundreds of kilometres away, and in good conditions perhaps much farther.
asks: Can whales hear each other across the ocean?
How far do blue whale calls go?

faq.a: Male humpback whales sing long, repeating songs in the breeding season, probably to attract females or compete with rivals. Other whales use calls to keep in touch with their group.

faq.q: Why does sound travel so far underwater?
faq.a: Water carries sound well and loses little energy from low notes, and the SOFAR channel stops sound escaping. Light, by contrast, is absorbed within a few hundred metres.
asks: Why do whales use sound and not sight?

faq.q: Why are whale calls so low?
faq.a: Low-pitched sounds lose much less energy as they travel than high-pitched ones, so they carry farther. The biggest whales make calls around 20 vibrations a second, near the bottom of human hearing.
asks: Why do blue whales make low sounds?
Can people hear blue whale calls?

facts: Sound travels about 1,500 metres per second in seawater, more than four times faster than in air.
The SOFAR channel was discovered in the 1940s by American scientists including Maurice Ewing.
Fin and blue whale calls are often around 20 hertz or lower, near or below the bottom of human hearing.

quiz.say: What happens to sound in the ocean's SOFAR channel?

options.show: Keeps bending back in, so it travels very far
options.say: Keeps bending back in, so it travels very far

quiz.why: Sound is slowest in that layer, so sound waves curve back into it from above and below and stay trapped, travelling great distances.

wrong.0: The channel helps sound travel, it does not stop it.
wrong.2: Sound in the channel bends back down instead of escaping to the surface.
